Is anybody sitting here? Thanks. I'm Stephen — Chicago. Two hours early, as always. My wife says I was born in a departure lounge.
Please, go ahead. I'm Rosângela, from São Paulo. We're the same — we've been at this gate since two o'clock.
Brazil! And how long have you been in Portugal?
For twelve days. Lisbon, then the north, then two nights in Porto. We've been coming to Europe since 2019, but this one was different.
Different how? Better hotels?
No — I did all the talking. My husband doesn't speak English, and for years I relied on my son for everything. I've only studied English for ten months.
Ten months? I assumed you'd spoken it all your life. Honestly, I've lived in Chicago for sixty-one years and my Spanish is still four words.
Well — step by step. I've come a long way, and I'm proud of it. Next year, three weeks. That's the goal.
How long have you been in Portugal?
We've been here since Monday, twelve days in all.

I used to rely on my son. Now I manage on my own.

My name is Andrew, and I am the night manager of a small hotel in Lisbon. I have stood behind the same front desk since two thousand and three, so that is twenty-two years of watching people arrive at eleven at night with a suitcase and a face. And I am going to tell you something I have never said to a guest. I can tell in about ten seconds which of them are traveling on their own. It has nothing to do with who is alone. Couples arrive, families arrive, groups of six arrive. What I watch is where the eyes go when I start speaking. Some guests look at me. Some guests look at the person beside them, and wait. And when that happens, I end up giving the information to the wrong pair of ears, because the person who is listening is not the person who is going to walk out of that door tomorrow morning and look for the tram. The trip belongs to whoever is listening. That is not always the person who paid for the room. Now, the part that took me twenty years to understand. Guests come back. Not many, but some, three years later, five years later, and here is what I notice about their English. It is the same. The same small mistakes, the same missing words, the same slow start. Nothing improved, and it made no difference at all. Because the second time, they ask me the question themselves, and they stay for the answer, and they ask a second one. That is the whole change. Not better grammar. A different pair of eyes.

It is Teresa again. I am the one who rehearsed her whole journey out loud in her kitchen, to nobody, two weeks before her first trip alone. Well, I went. And I have been home for two weeks now, and I want to tell you what really happened, because it is not what I expected. I used almost none of the sentences I rehearsed. Almost none of them. The airport did not go the way I had practiced, the shuttle was in a different place, the woman at passport control asked me something about my return ticket that I had never thought about. And I want to say clearly that this was not a problem, because it took me a few days to understand why. The rehearsal was never a script. The rehearsal was practice at opening my mouth. On the second day, the hotel had no record of my booking. None. I had never practiced that sentence, not once, and I said it badly, in the wrong order, with the wrong verb, twice. And the woman at the desk understood me anyway and found the reservation under my first name. Twenty minutes, and it was over, and I went upstairs, and I sat on the bed and I laughed. So here is what I do now. I have already booked the next trip, for the spring. And I still stand in my kitchen for twenty minutes a day and speak English to nobody, and my daughter still thinks I have lost my mind. Keep it up after the lessons stop. That is the only thing I have to say. The lessons end. The traveler does not.
